what_it_does: Fault-tolerant quantum computers protect fragile quantum bits from errors by spreading each logical qubit across many physical qubits — but this protection scheme requires a lot of overhead space just for routing and accessing those qubits, eating up roughly half of all available qubit slots. LSQCA (Load/Store Quantum Computer Architecture) borrows a trick from classical computer design: it separates qubit storage into a small, fast-access region (like CPU registers) and a large, slower storage area (like main memory). Most qubits sit in the slow region most of the time; only a few are moved to the fast region when they are actually being computed on. Because programs tend to reuse the same qubits repeatedly in bursts (locality), the delay of moving qubits in and out can often be hidden by overlapping it with other work, recovering much of the capacity lost to routing overhead.
